proposals.after: When the Supreme Clarity Palace was completed, Court Director Wei Tao composed six tunes—"Jingyun," "Nine Perfections," "Purple Pole," "Little Longevity," "Receiving Heaven," and "Following Heaven Music"—and also composed the shang-mode tune "Ruler and Minister Meeting in Joy."
proposals.reason: Matches the idiomatic repair for 縚 → Tao.

proposals.before: After Daizong retook the capitals with Prince of Guangping, Pear Garden officer Liu Rijin offered eighteen Precious Response Long Peace pieces, all in palace mode.
proposals.after: When Daizong, as Prince of Guangping, recovered the two capitals, Pear Garden officer Liu Rijin offered eighteen Precious Response Long Peace pieces, all in palace mode.
proposals.reason: 代宗繇廣平王 means Daizong acting from his prior title Prince of Guangping (same person), not two people retaking the capitals together.

proposals.before: Xuanzong's ministerial banquets always featured the full hundred acts.
proposals.after: Xuānzong's ministerial banquets always featured the full hundred acts.
proposals.reason: 宣宗 is Xuānzong, distinct from 玄宗 (Xuánzong); undifferentiated "Xuanzong" confuses the two Tang emperors.

decisions.reason: Chinese 沈珫 gives the personal name Shen Chong (珫 chōng); Kuang is a wrong reading. The proposed idiomatic line corrects only that given name.
Chinese 沈珫 is Shen Chong (珫 chōng); the literal's Shen Kuang is the same misreading. The proposed replacement restores Chong and leaves the rest unchanged.
Chinese 王廞 is Wang Xin (廞 xīn); Yin is a wrong reading of the given name. The proposed idiomatic line corrects only that name.
Chinese 王廞 is Wang Xin (廞 xīn); the literal's Wang Yin is the same misreading. The proposed replacement restores Xin without other changes.
Chinese 宋隨王誕 is Song Prince of Sui Dan: 王 is the princely title in 隨王, and 誕 is the personal name. "Wang Dan" wrongly treats 王 as a surname; dropping Wang restores the Chinese.
Chinese 韋縚 is Wei Tao (縚 tāo); Yun is a wrong reading. The proposed idiomatic line corrects only that personal name.
Chinese 韋縚 is Wei Tao (縚 tāo); the literal's Wei Yun is the same misreading. The proposed replacement restores Tao and leaves the rest intact.

Chinese 代宗繇廣平王復二京 uses 繇 "from/as" so Daizong, from his prior title Prince of Guangping, recovered the two capitals—one person, not Daizong together with another Prince of Guangping. The proposed idiomatic wording restores that identity.
Chinese 宣宗 is Xuānzong, not the better-known 玄宗 (Xuánzong); undiacriticized Xuanzong conflates the two. Context (大中) confirms 宣宗, and the proposed tone-marked Xuānzong correctly disambiguates.
